claim: The bacterial flagellar motor can rotate the flagellar filament at high speed.
source: The bacterial flagellar motor is a molecular machine that can rotate the flagellar filament at high speed.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract describing the flagellar motor function.

claim: The rotation of the flagellar motor is generated by the stator–rotor interaction, coupled with an ion flux through the torque-generating stator.
source: The rotation is generated by the stator–rotor interaction, coupled with an ion flux through the torque-generating stator.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established understanding.

claim: Cryo-electron tomography was employed to visualize the intact flagellar motor in Borrelia burgdorferi.
source: Here we employed cryo-electron tomography to visualize the intact flagellar motor in the Lyme disease spirochete, Borrelia burgdorferi.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The stator complex was localized in situ by analyzing motor structures of wild-type and stator-deletion mutants.
source: By analyzing the motor structures of wild-type and stator-deletion mutants, we not only localized the stator complex in situ, but also revealed the stator–rotor interaction at an unprecedented detail.
evidence: This describes the findings from comparative structural analysis.

claim: The stator–rotor interaction induces a conformational change in the flagella C-ring.
source: Importantly, the stator–rotor interaction induces a conformational change in the flagella C-ring.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: A non-motile mutant in which proton flux is blocked cannot generate the conformational change observed in wild-type.
source: Given our observation that a non-motile mutant, in which proton flux is blocked, cannot generate the similar conformational change, we propose that the proton-driven torque is responsible for the conformational change required for flagellar rotation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the abstract.

claim: The proton-driven torque is responsible for the conformational change required for flagellar rotation.
source: Given our observation that a non-motile mutant, in which proton flux is blocked, cannot generate the similar conformational change, we propose that the proton-driven torque is responsible for the conformational change required for flagellar rotation.
evidence: This is proposed based on the observations from mutant analysis.

claim: Many bacterial pathogens require motility to infect, disseminate, and cause disease in humans and other mammalian hosts.
source: Many bacterial pathogens require motility to infect, disseminate, and cause disease in humans and other mammalian hosts.
evidence: This is general background knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: The flagellum consists of a motor, hook, and long filament.
source: The flagellum consists of a motor, hook, and long filament (Macnab, 2003; Terashima et al., 2008; Berg, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The motor is a sophisticated nanomachine composed of a rotor and a stator.
source: The motor is a sophisticated nanomachine composed of a rotor, which is the rotary part, and a stator, which surrounds the rotor.
evidence: This is general knowledge about motor structure.

claim: The rotation of the motor is driven by the interaction between the rotor and the stator, which is powered by the proton or sodium gradient across the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: The rotation of the motor is driven by the interaction between the rotor and the stator, which is powered by the proton or sodium gradient across the cytoplasmic membrane (Berg, 2003; Sowa and Berry, 2008; Minamino et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: How the ion gradient couples the mechanical rotation remains elusive at the molecular level.
source: However, how the ion gradient couples the mechanical rotation remains elusive at the molecular level.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Each stator complex is composed of two transmembrane proteins: MotA and MotB.
source: Each stator complex is composed of two transmembrane proteins: MotA and MotB (Braun and Blair, 2001; Kojima and Blair, 2004a; Sato and Homma, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MotA has a large cytoplasmic domain, which contains conserved charged residues that are critical for the interaction with the rotor-associated protein FliG.
source: MotA has a large cytoplasmic domain, which contains conserved charged residues that are critical for the interaction with the rotor-associated protein FliG (Zhou and Blair, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MotB has a large periplasmic domain that is believed to bind to the peptidoglycan layer.
source: MotB has a large periplasmic domain that is believed to bind to the peptidoglycan layer (Chun and Parkinson, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Stator complexes in some motors are constantly exchanged with those in the membrane pool.
source: However, stator complexes in some motor are constantly exchanged with those in the membrane pool (Leake et al., 2006), resulting in the dynamic nature and variable assembly of the stator complexes (Block and Berg, 1984; Blair and Berg, 1988; Reid et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The assembly of the stator is mediated by ion flow in E. coli and Vibrio alginolyticus.
source: The assembly of the stator is mediated by ion flow in E. coli and Vibrio alginolyticus (Tipping et al., 2013; Fukuoka et al., 2009), as its disruption leads to reversible stator complex diffusion away from the motor.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A conserved aspartic acid residue in the transmembrane segment of MotB (D32 in E. coli and D33 in S. enterica) is the predicted proton-binding site and plays a crucial role for torque generation and bacterial motility.
source: A conserved aspartic acid residue in the transmembrane segment of MotB (D32 in E. coli and D33 in S. enterica) is the predicted proton-binding site and plays a crucial role for torque generation and bacterial motility (Zhou et al., 1998a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Proton binding/dissociation at the conserved aspartic acid residue triggers conformational changes in the cytoplasmic domain of MotA to produce a power-stroke on the C-ring that drives flagellar rotation.
source: It is thought that proton binding/dissociation at this residue triggers conformational changes in the cytoplasmic domain of MotA to produce a power-stroke on the C-ring that drives flagellar rotation (Kojima and Blair, 2001).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: Electron micrographs of freeze-fractured membrane showed the stator complexes as stud-like particles in E. coli, Streptococcus, and Aquaspirillum serpens.
source: Electron micrographs of freeze-fractured membrane showed the stator complexes as stud-like particles in E. coli, Streptococcus, and Aquaspirillum serpens (Khan et al., 1988; Coulton and Murray, 1978).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Electron microscopy of purified PomA/PomB revealed two arm-like periplasmic domains and a large cytoplasmic domain.
source: Recently, electron microscopy of purified PomA/PomB (a MotA/MotB homolog) revealed two arm-like periplasmic domains and a large cytoplasmic domain (Yonekura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Detailed visualization of stator units remains challenging in many bacterial species including E. coli and S. enterica, because the stator complexes are highly dynamic and wild type cells are often too large for high resolution cryo-ET imaging.
source: However, detailed visualization of stator units remains challenging in many bacterial species including E. coli and S. enterica, because the stator complexes are highly dynamic and wild type cells are often too large for high resolution cryo-ET imaging.
evidence: This explains technical challenges in the field.

claim: Stator complexes have been observed in many intact flagellar motors, including spirochetal flagellar motors and polar flagellar motors.
source: In contrast, stator complexes have been observed in many intact flagellar motors, including spirochetal flagellar motors (Chen et al., 2011; Murphy et al., 2006; Kudryashev et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2010a; Zhao et al., 2014) and polar flagellar motors (Beeby et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The flagella in B. burgdorferi are enclosed between the outer membrane and the peptidoglycan layer and are thus called periplasmic flagella.
source: The flagella in B. burgdorferi are enclosed between the outer membrane and the peptidoglycan layer and are thus called periplasmic flagella.
evidence: This describes the unique structure of B. burgdorferi flagella.

claim: The flagellar motors in B. burgdorferi are found at both cell poles and rotate coordinately to enable the cell to run, pause, or flex.
source: The flagellar motors are found at both cell poles and rotate coordinately to enable the cell to run, pause, or flex (Charon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The rotations of periplasmic flagella cause the cell to form a flat-wave shape to efficiently bore its way through tissue and viscous environments.
source: The rotations of periplasmic flagella cause the cell to form a flat-wave shape to efficiently bore its way through tissue and viscous environments (Charon et al., 2012; Moriarty et al., 2008; Motaleb et al., 2000; Motaleb et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The B. burgdorferi motor differs in some aspects from the E. coli motor, such as the presence of a prominent 'collar' structure.
source: Although the B. burgdorferi motor differs in some aspects from the E. coli motor (e.g. the presence of a prominent 'collar' structure), genome sequence analyses as well as in situ structural analyses suggest that the major flagellar components are remarkably similar to those of other bacterial species (Qin et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The major flagellar components in B. burgdorferi are remarkably similar to those of other bacterial species.
source: Although the B. burgdorferi motor differs in some aspects from the E. coli motor (e.g. the presence of a prominent 'collar' structure), genome sequence analyses as well as in situ structural analyses suggest that the major flagellar components are remarkably similar to those of other bacterial species (Qin et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Membrane protein FliL was identified as an important player that controls periplasmic flagellar orientation.
source: Furthermore, membrane protein FliL was identified as an important player that controls periplasmic flagellar orientation (Motaleb et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The collar plays an important role in recruiting and stabilizing the stator complexes.
source: More recently, the collar (a spirochete-specific feature) was determined to play an important role in recruiting and stabilizing the stator complexes (Moon et al., 2016; Moon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Wild-type B. burgdorferi cells were immobilized after being treated with proton uncoupler CCCP.
source: Previous studies have shown that wild-type (WT) B. burgdorferi cells were immobilized after being treated with proton uncoupler Carbonyl cyanide 3-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP), indicating that the proton gradient is used for flagellar rotation (Motaleb et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The proton gradient is used for flagellar rotation in B. burgdorferi.
source: Previous studies have shown that wild-type (WT) B. burgdorferi cells were immobilized after being treated with proton uncoupler Carbonyl cyanide 3-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP), indicating that the proton gradient is used for flagellar rotation (Motaleb et al., 2000).
evidence: This is inferred from the CCCP treatment experiment cited.

claim: ΔmotB cells were completely non-motile.
source: As ΔmotB cells were completely non-motile (Sultan et al., 2015), and both motA and motB genes are located in the middle of the flgB operon in B. burgdorferi (Figure 1A), the MotA/MotB complex is the torque generating unit essential for spirochetal motility, though not for flagellar assembly (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The MotA/MotB complex is the torque generating unit essential for spirochetal motility, though not for flagellar assembly.
source: As ΔmotB cells were completely non-motile (Sultan et al., 2015), and both motA and motB genes are located in the middle of the flgB operon in B. burgdorferi (Figure 1A), the MotA/MotB complex is the torque generating unit essential for spirochetal motility, though not for flagellar assembly (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is inferred from the non-motile phenotype of ΔmotB cells and the presence of flagella.

claim: Both ΔmotA and ΔmotB mutant cells are non-motile and have irregular and rod-shaped morphology.
source: We constructed deletion mutants ΔmotB and ΔmotA, showing that both mutant cells are non-motile and have irregular and rod-shaped morphology − very different from the highly motile wave-like WT or complemented motBcom cells (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the constructed mutants and shown in figures.

claim: Both ΔmotA and ΔmotB cells possess paralyzed flagella.
source: Both ΔmotA and ΔmotB cells possess paralyzed flagella, indicating that both mutants lack the torque-generating unit (Figure 1D), which is consistent with the notion that MotA and MotB form a stator complex necessary for torque generation (Kojima and Blair, 2004b).
evidence: This is observed in the mutants and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Aspartic acid in MotB (B. burgdorferi Asp-24, E. coli Asp-32, and S. enterica Asp-33) is highly conserved.
source: Aspartic acid in MotB (B. burgdorferi Asp-24, E. coli Asp-32, and S. enterica Asp-33) is highly conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and it is thought to be directly involved in proton translocation in E. coli and S. enterica (Zhou et al., 1998a; Che et al., 2008).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and supported by citations.

claim: The conserved aspartic acid in MotB is thought to be directly involved in proton translocation in E. coli and S. enterica.
source: Aspartic acid in MotB (B. burgdorferi Asp-24, E. coli Asp-32, and S. enterica Asp-33) is highly conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and it is thought to be directly involved in proton translocation in E. coli and S. enterica (Zhou et al., 1998a; Che et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: motB-D24E mutant cells are less motile than the WT cells.
source: Dark-field microscopy and swarm plate motility assays indicated that motB-D24E mutant cells are less motile than the WT cells whereas motB-D24N cells are completely non-motile (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dark-field microscopy and swarm plate assays shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: motB-D24N cells are completely non-motile.
source: Dark-field microscopy and swarm plate motility assays indicated that motB-D24E mutant cells are less motile than the WT cells whereas motB-D24N cells are completely non-motile (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by dark-field microscopy and swarm plate assays shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The result obtained with motB-D24E is consistent with the reduced motility observed with the D32E substitution in E. coli MotB.
source: The result obtained with motB-D24E is consistent with the reduced motility observed with the D32E substitution in E. coli MotB (Zhou et al., 1998a) and the D33E substitution in S. enterica (Che et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The non-motile phenotype in B. burgdorferi motB-D24N is identical to that of the D32N substitution in E. coli MotB.
source: The non-motile phenotype in B. burgdorferi motB-D24N is also identical to that of the D32N substitution in E. coli MotB (Zhou et al., 1998a; Blair et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The MotA/MotB complex is the torque-generating unit in B. burgdorferi.
source: Therefore, we concluded that the MotA/MotB complex is the torque-generating unit in B. burgdorferi, and Asp-24 in MotB is essential for proton translocation.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutant phenotypes and comparison with other species.

claim: Asp-24 in MotB is essential for proton translocation in B. burgdorferi.
source: Therefore, we concluded that the MotA/MotB complex is the torque-generating unit in B. burgdorferi, and Asp-24 in MotB is essential for proton translocation.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutant phenotypes and comparison with other species.

claim: The averaged structures of the motors in the ΔmotB and ΔmotA mutants exhibited many of the same features as the WT motor, such as the export apparatus, the C-ring, the MS-ring, the rod, the P-ring, and the spirochete-specific periplasmic collar.
source: The averaged structures of the motors in the ΔmotB and ΔmotA mutants exhibited many of the same features as the WT motor, such as the export apparatus, the C-ring, the MS-ring, the rod, the P-ring, and the spirochete-specific periplasmic collar.
evidence: This is observed from the asymmetric reconstructions.

claim: Both ΔmotA and ΔmotB mutants lacked large transmembrane densities peripheral to the C-ring compared to the WT motor structure.
source: However, juxtaposed with the WT motor structure, both ΔmotA and ΔmotB mutants lacked large transmembrane densities peripheral to the C-ring (indicated by arrows in Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Complementation of ΔmotB restored the missing densities of the ΔmotB mutant.
source: Complementation of ΔmotB restored the missing densities of the ΔmotB mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and also restored WT motility and cell morphology (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The peripheral densities in the WT motor are comprised of MotA/MotB complexes.
source: These results suggest that the peripheral densities in the WT motor are comprised of MotA/MotB complexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion and complementation experiments.

claim: Sixteen stator densities are symmetrically distributed around the C-ring in each WT motor.
source: In each WT motor, sixteen of these densities are symmetrically distributed around the C-ring (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2E.

claim: The stator ring has 16-fold symmetry and ~80 nm diameter.
source: They form a stator ring with 16-fold symmetry and ~80 nm diameter, which is significantly larger than the ΔmotB mutant's C-ring diameter of ~57 nm (Figure 2E, Video 1).
evidence: This is measured from the structure shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The ΔmotB mutant's C-ring diameter is ~57 nm.
source: They form a stator ring with 16-fold symmetry and ~80 nm diameter, which is significantly larger than the ΔmotB mutant's C-ring diameter of ~57 nm (Figure 2E, Video 1).
evidence: This is measured from the structure.

claim: The bottom portion of the WT C-ring has the same diameter of 56 nm as the ΔmotB mutant.
source: Compared to the C-ring in the ΔmotB mutant, the bottom portion of the WT C-ring has the same diameter of 56 nm, while the top portion undergoes considerable changes in the presence of the stator complexes.
evidence: This is measured from the structures.

claim: The top portion of the WT C-ring undergoes considerable changes in the presence of the stator complexes.
source: Compared to the C-ring in the ΔmotB mutant, the bottom portion of the WT C-ring has the same diameter of 56 nm, while the top portion undergoes considerable changes in the presence of the stator complexes.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures.

claim: The diameter of the C-ring reduces from 59 nm in the ΔmotB to 57 nm in the WT.
source: Specifically, the diameter of the C-ring reduces from 59 nm in the ΔmotB to 57 nm in the WT (Figure 2B and E).
evidence: This is measured from the structures shown in Figure 2B and E.

claim: Both C-ring and collar are modulated by the curved membrane in both ∆motB and WT motors.
source: As the motor is embedded in the cytoplasmic membrane, both C-ring and collar are apparently modulated by the curved membrane in both ∆motB (Figure 3A–C) and WT motors (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3A–F.

claim: The 16-fold symmetry of the collar is well preserved.
source: Although the 16-fold symmetry of the collar is well preserved (Figure 3B,C), the symmetry of the C-ring is not obvious in the ΔmotB mutant, indicating that there a mismatch between the C-ring and the collar.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3B,C.

claim: The symmetry of the C-ring is not obvious in the ΔmotB mutant.
source: Although the 16-fold symmetry of the collar is well preserved (Figure 3B,C), the symmetry of the C-ring is not obvious in the ΔmotB mutant, indicating that there a mismatch between the C-ring and the collar.
evidence: This is observed in the structure.

claim: There is a mismatch between the C-ring and the collar in the ΔmotB mutant.
source: Although the 16-fold symmetry of the collar is well preserved (Figure 3B,C), the symmetry of the C-ring is not obvious in the ΔmotB mutant, indicating that there a mismatch between the C-ring and the collar.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of obvious C-ring symmetry.

claim: The C-ring in the WT motor has a 46-fold symmetry.
source: Indeed, a combination of asymmetric reconstruction and focused alignment allows us to show for the first time that the C-ring in the WT motor has a 46-fold symmetry (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), while the surrounding stator ring and the collar have a 16-fold symmetry (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is determined by asymmetric reconstruction and focused alignment shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The surrounding stator ring and the collar have a 16-fold symmetry in the WT motor.
source: Indeed, a combination of asymmetric reconstruction and focused alignment allows us to show for the first time that the C-ring in the WT motor has a 46-fold symmetry (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), while the surrounding stator ring and the collar have a 16-fold symmetry (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The sixteen stator complexes in the WT motor display considerable variation in height as they are embedded in the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: Importantly, the sixteen stator complexes in the WT motor also display considerable variation in height as they are embedded in the cytoplasmic membrane and their periplasmic domains are inserted between the collar (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3H.

claim: The stator complex is composed of a periplasmic portion and a cytoplasmic portion.
source: The stator complex is composed of a periplasmic portion and a cytoplasmic portion (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3I and J.

claim: The periplasmic portion of the stator complex is ~14 nm in height.
source: The periplasmic portion is ~14 nm in height, and it directly interacts with the collar and FliL (Figure 3I), which have been previously identified as periplasmic structures (Motaleb et al., 2011).
evidence: This is measured from the structure shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The periplasmic portion of the stator complex directly interacts with the collar and FliL.
source: The periplasmic portion is ~14 nm in height, and it directly interacts with the collar and FliL (Figure 3I), which have been previously identified as periplasmic structures (Motaleb et al., 2011).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3I and supported by citation.

claim: The interactions between the stator and collar/FliL are believed to play critical roles in stabilizing the stator.
source: The interactions are believed to play critical roles in stabilizing the stator, as the lack of FliL or collar proteins has a profound impact on stator assembly and motility (Motaleb et al., 2011; Moon et al., 2016; Moon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The collar-FliL assembly exhibits conformational changes due to the absence or presence of the stator complexes.
source: Notably, the collar-FliL assembly also exhibits conformational changes due to the absence or presence of the stator complexes (Figure 3H,J), further confirming protein-protein interactions among the stator complex and the collar (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 3H,J.

claim: The cytoplasmic portion of the stator complex is ~8 nm in diameter.
source: The cytoplasmic portion of the stator complex is ~8 nm in diameter, which is comparable to the structure observed in the freeze-fractured membrane (Khan et al., 1988; Coulton and Murray, 1978; Khan et al., 1992), and is adjacent to the top portion of the C-ring (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is measured from the structure shown in Figure 3I and compared with previous literature.

claim: The interaction between the stator and the C-ring induces a noticeable conformational change in the C-ring.
source: Importantly, the interaction between the stator and the C-ring induces a noticeable conformational change in the C-ring (Figure 3I), compared to that in the ∆motB mutant motor (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is observed by comparing Figure 3I and Figure 3G.

claim: The top of the C-ring appears to be tilted toward the MS-ring by ~6° in the presence of the stator complex.
source: The top of the C-ring appears to be tilted toward the MS-ring by ~6° in the presence of the stator complex (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is measured from the structure shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The local conformational change is consistent with the overall diameter change of the C-ring observed in ∆motB and WT motors.
source: Importantly, this local conformational change is consistent with the overall diameter change of the C-ring (Figure 2B,E) observed in ∆motB and WT motors.
evidence: This is inferred by comparing the local and overall changes.

claim: Both the motB-D24E and motB-D24N mutants have stator complexes assembled in the motor.
source: Both the motB-D24E and motB-D24N mutants have stator complexes assembled in the motor (Figure 4A–D), but the stator densities are significantly weaker than that in WT cells (by comparing Figure 4A–D with Figure 2D), suggesting that the stator complexes vary in their location or occupancy.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4A–D.

claim: The stator densities in motB-D24E and motB-D24N mutants are significantly weaker than that in WT cells.
source: Both the motB-D24E and motB-D24N mutants have stator complexes assembled in the motor (Figure 4A–D), but the stator densities are significantly weaker than that in WT cells (by comparing Figure 4A–D with Figure 2D), suggesting that the stator complexes vary in their location or occupancy.
evidence: This is observed by comparing Figure 4A–D with Figure 2D.

claim: Stator occupancy is 97.0% in WT cells, suggesting that there are ~16 stator complexes in each WT motor.
source: Statistical analysis of the stator complexes (details described in the Materials and Methods section) shows that stator occupancy is 97.0% in WT cells, suggesting that there are ~16 stator complexes in each WT motor.
evidence: This is calculated from statistical analysis of the structures.

claim: In the motB-D24E motor, stator occupancy is ~62.5%, suggesting that there are ~10 stator complexes in each motor on average.
source: In the motB-D24E motor, stator occupancy is ~62.5%, suggesting that there are ~10 stator complexes in each motor on average.
evidence: This is calculated from statistical analysis of the structures.

claim: In motB-D24N, it is estimated that there are ~7 stator complexes in each motor on average.
source: In motB-D24N, it is estimated that there are ~7 stator complexes in each motor on average (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is calculated from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reduced stator occupancy in motB-D24E and motB-D24N mutants is consistent with the notion that the proton gradient affects stator assembly and stability.
source: As these two residue substitutions are known to respectively reduce or block proton flux in the stator complex, reduced stator occupancy in these mutants is consistent with the notion that the proton gradient affects stator assembly and stability (Tipping et al., 2013; Fukuoka et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The C-ring in the motB-D24N motor undergoes a minor change in the presence of the stator complex compared to the ∆motB motor's C-ring.
source: Importantly, compared to the ∆motB motor's C-ring (Figure 4E), that in the motB-D24N motor undergoes a minor change in the presence of the stator complex (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is observed by comparing Figure 4E and Figure 4F.

claim: The proton channel is likely blocked in the motB-D24N motor.
source: As the proton channel is likely blocked in the motB-D24N motor, no torque is generated by the stator complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the D24N mutation known to block proton flux.

claim: No torque is generated by the stator complex in the motB-D24N motor.
source: As the proton channel is likely blocked in the motB-D24N motor, no torque is generated by the stator complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the blocked proton channel.

claim: The C-ring conformation in the motB-D24N is similar to that in the ∆motB motor.
source: As a result, the C-ring conformation in the motB-D24N is similar to that in the ∆motB motor.
evidence: This is observed from the similar tilt angles.

claim: All 16 stator complexes remained associated with the motor after 15 min of treatment with CCCP.
source: To further examine the impact of the proton gradient on the C-ring, we analyzed the nonmotile WT motors after 15 min of treatment with CCCP. All 16 stator complexes remained associated with the motor (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tilt angle of the C-ring was 5.1° in CCCP-treated WT motors, which is different from that in the motile WT motor.
source: However, the tilt angle of the C-ring was 5.1°, which is different from that in the motile WT motor (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is measured from the structure shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conformational change of the C-ring likely results from the torque generated by the proton gradient.
source: Therefore, the conformational change of the C-ring likely results from the torque generated by the proton gradient.
evidence: This is inferred from the CCCP treatment experiment.

claim: There is a noticeable difference in tilt angles of the C-ring between the motB-D24E motor (3.2°) and the ∆motB motor (7.8°).
source: There is a noticeable difference in tilt angles of the C-ring between the motB-D24E motor (3.2° Figure 4G) and the ∆motB motor (7.8° in Figure 4E).
evidence: This is measured from the structures shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4E.

claim: The residue substitution D24E was known to reduce proton flux.
source: As the residue substitution D24E was known to reduce proton flux, we expected there to be less torque generated by the stator complex.
evidence: This is supported by previous literature on similar mutations.

claim: There was less conformational change in the motB-D24E motor when compared to WT cells.
source: Although we were not able to directly measure the torque, we provide evidence that there was less conformational change in the motB-D24E motor when compared to WT cells.
evidence: This is observed from the tilt angle measurements.

claim: The conformational change of the C-ring correlated with the proton flux transmitting through the stator channel.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that the conformational change of the C-ring correlated with the proton flux transmitting through the stator channel.
evidence: This is concluded from the data on different mutants.

claim: The FliN tetramer was placed into the bulge at the bottom of the C-ring, as proposed for E. coli.
source: The FliN tetramer was placed into the bulge at the bottom of the C-ring, as proposed for E. coli (Brown et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on a model proposed for E. coli cited in the literature.

claim: 46 FliG proteins are organized in a ring in the WT motor.
source: The densities were well-fitted with 46 FliG proteins organized in a ring in our EM map (Figure 5, Video 2).
evidence: This is determined by fitting crystal structures into the EM map shown in Figure 5.

claim: FliG proteins are relatively far away from the periphery of the MS-ring in the ΔmotB motor, and the C-ring appears to be disengaged from the MS-ring.
source: Noticeably, FliG proteins are relatively far away from the periphery of the MS-ring, and the C-ring appears to be disengaged from the MS-ring.
evidence: This is observed from the model shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the WT motor, the FliG/FliN/FliM complex has to be rotated for about ~6° to fit into the C-ring density.
source: In the WT motor, the FliG/FliN/FliM complex has to be rotated for about ~6° to fit into the C-ring density (Figure 5, Video 2).
evidence: This is determined by fitting the complex into the EM density shown in Figure 5.

claim: The additional shifts of the FliG proteins enables the C-ring to engage with the MS-ring at its periphery.
source: The additional shifts of the FliG proteins enables the C-ring to engage with the MS-ring at its periphery.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model.

claim: The N-terminal domain of FliG interacts with the periphery of the MS-ring in the WT motor.
source: As a result, the N-terminal domain of FliG interacts with the periphery of the MS-ring, and the C-terminal domain of FliG interacts with the stator.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model.

claim: The C-terminal domain of FliG interacts with the stator in the WT motor.
source: As a result, the N-terminal domain of FliG interacts with the periphery of the MS-ring, and the C-terminal domain of FliG interacts with the stator.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model.

claim: Several charged residues in FliG and MotA are important for torque generation in E. coli.
source: It has been demonstrated that several charged residues in FliG and MotA are important for torque generation in E. coli (Zhou and Blair, 1997; Zhou et al., 1998b; Lloyd et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two charged residues in the C-terminal domain of FliG are adjacent to the cytoplasmic portion of the stator complexes.
source: Consistent with these findings, our model shows that two charged residues in the C-terminal domain of FliG are adjacent to the cytoplasmic portion of the stator complexes, which presumably interact with the charged residues of MotA (Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 5.

claim: Powered by the proton gradient, the stator–rotor interactions induce a large conformational change of the C-ring, consequently driving flagellar rotation.
source: Powered by the proton gradient, the stator–rotor interactions induce a large conformational change of the C-ring, consequently driving flagellar rotation.
evidence: This is the proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The periplasmic collar constitutes a large, turbine-like complex in the flagellar motor of spirochetes.
source: The periplasmic collar constitutes a large, turbine-like complex in the flagellar motor of spirochetes.
evidence: This is a description of the collar structure.

claim: The collar plays an important role in the assembly of periplasmic flagella, and hence, in determining cell morphology and motility.
source: This structure plays an important role in the assembly of periplasmic flagella, and hence, in determining cell morphology and motility (Moon et al., 2016; Moon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sixteen stator complexes in B. burgdorferi appear to be stably assembled around the collar.
source: In contrast to the highly dynamic stator complexes in the E. coli flagellar motor, sixteen stator complexes in B. burgdorferi appear to be stably assembled around the collar (Figure 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 2 and Figure 3.

claim: In the absence of the collar, the stator complexes were no longer visible in sub-tomogram averages.
source: In the absence of the collar, the stator complexes were no longer visible in sub-tomogram averages, suggesting that the collar is important for assembling and stabilizing the stator in B. burgdorferi (Moon et al., 2016; Moon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The collar is important for assembling and stabilizing the stator in B. burgdorferi.
source: In the absence of the collar, the stator complexes were no longer visible in sub-tomogram averages, suggesting that the collar is important for assembling and stabilizing the stator in B. burgdorferi (Moon et al., 2016; Moon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of stator complexes when collar is deleted, supported by citations.

claim: FliL forms additional periplasmic structures between the stator and the collar.
source: In addition, FliL forms additional periplasmic structures between the stator and the collar (Motaleb et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of fliL resulted in cells with defects in motility.
source: Deletion of fliL resulted in cells with defects in motility (Motaleb et al., 2011) and a flagellar motor with fewer stator units (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that FliL also plays an important role in stator assembly in B. burgdorferi.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Deletion of fliL resulted in a flagellar motor with fewer stator units.
source: Deletion of fliL resulted in cells with defects in motility (Motaleb et al., 2011) and a flagellar motor with fewer stator units (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that FliL also plays an important role in stator assembly in B. burgdorferi.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: FliL plays an important role in stator assembly in B. burgdorferi.
source: Deletion of fliL resulted in cells with defects in motility (Motaleb et al., 2011) and a flagellar motor with fewer stator units (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 3), suggesting that FliL also plays an important role in stator assembly in B. burgdorferi.
evidence: This is inferred from the deletion phenotype.

claim: The proton gradient is essential for flagellar rotation.
source: The proton gradient is not only essential for flagellar rotation but also critical for assembly of the stators around the motor in E. coli and other model systems.
evidence: This is general knowledge about flagellar motors.

claim: The proton gradient is critical for assembly of the stators around the motor in E. coli and other model systems.
source: The proton gradient is not only essential for flagellar rotation but also critical for assembly of the stators around the motor in E. coli and other model systems.
evidence: This is general knowledge about flagellar motors.

claim: The average number of stator units decreased significantly in the less motile motB-D24E (65% occupancy) and non-motile motB-D24N (45% occupancy) motors.
source: By altering the putative proton channel in B. burgdorferi, we found that the average number of stator units decreased significantly in the less motile motB-D24E (65% occupancy) and non-motile motB-D24N (45% occupancy) motors (Figure 4).
evidence: This is measured from the structures shown in Figure 4.

claim: Even in the non-motile motB-D24N cells, some stator units remained associated with the motor.
source: However, even in the non-motile motB-D24N cells, some stator units remained associated with the motor.
evidence: This is observed from the structural analysis.

claim: In E. coli and other model systems, stator units were found to dissociate from both Na+- and H+-driven motors when the ion motive force was disrupted.
source: This finding is different from the observations in E. coli and other model systems, in which stator units were found to dissociate from both Na+- and H+-driven motors when the ion motive force was disrupted (Tipping et al., 2013; Fukuoka et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The periplasmic collar in spirochetes may be the key reason underlying the difference in stator stability compared to E. coli.
source: The periplasmic collar in spirochetes may be the key reason underlying the difference, as deletion of genes that encode the proteins of the collar also disrupt the assembly of the stator units (Moon et al., 2016; Moon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the collar's role in stator assembly, supported by citations.

claim: Proton flow through the motor triggers conformational changes in the stator that generate a power stroke to the C-ring.
source: It has been proposed that proton flow through the motor triggers conformational changes in the stator that generate a power stroke to the C-ring (Kojima and Blair, 2001).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: The conformational change of the C-ring from motB-D24N to motB-D24E is much more significant than that from ∆motB to motB-D24N.
source: Importantly, by comparing the structures of ∆motB, motB-D24N, and motB-D24E (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), we found that the conformational change of the C-ring from motB-D24N to motB-D24E (conformational change of the top portion and 3.4° tilt angle change) is much more significant than that from ∆motB to motB-D24N (no change of the top portion and only 1.2° tilt angle change).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the structures shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stator-binding alone is not sufficient to induce the large C-ring conformational changes.
source: This indicates that stator-binding alone is not sufficient to induce the large C-ring conformational changes because stator complexes associated with the motB-D24N motor are not able to interact effectively with the C-ring and drive flagellar rotation, as proton conduction is blocked in the motB-D24N motor.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of mutants.

claim: The torque induced by proton flux is required for the C-ring conformational changes and flagellar rotation.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the torque induced by proton flux is required for the C-ring conformational changes and flagellar rotation.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutant analysis.

claim: Before assembly of the stator complexes, the B. burgdorferi flagellar motor is composed of the MS-ring, the rod, the export apparatus, the collar with 16-fold symmetry, and the C-ring with 46-fold symmetry.
source: Before assembly of the stator complexes, the B. burgdorferi flagellar motor is composed of the MS-ring, the rod, the export apparatus, the collar with 16-fold symmetry, and the C-ring with 46-fold symmetry (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 6.

claim: The collar and the associated FliL protein provide 16 well-defined locations for the recruitment of stator complexes.
source: The collar and the associated FliL protein provide 16 well-defined locations for the recruitment of stator complexes, which assemble around the collar and the C-ring.
evidence: This is proposed based on the structural observations.

claim: Stator complexes with blocked proton conduction only partially occupy the 16 possible locations.
source: Stator complexes with blocked proton conduction only partially occupy the 16 possible locations (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 6.

claim: There is little conformational change in the C-ring at the stator–rotor interface when proton conduction is blocked.
source: There is little conformational change in the C-ring at the stator–rotor interface.
evidence: This is observed in the motB-D24N mutant.

claim: Larger conformational changes of the C-ring occur with higher torque generated by stator complexes with increasing proton-conduction capability.
source: Larger conformational changes of the C-ring occur with higher torque generated by stator complexes with increasing proton-conduction capability (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in the model in Figure 6 and inferred from the data.

claim: High resolution in situ structural analysis of the flagellar motor from wild-type and mutants in B. burgdorferi has provided new insights into the assembly of torque-generating stators and their interactions with other flagellar components.
source: In summary, high resolution in situ structural analysis of the flagellar motor from wild-type and mutant in B. burgdorferi has provided new insights into the assembly of torque-generating stators and their interactions with other flagellar components in both the periplasm and cytoplasm.
evidence: This summarizes the findings of the study.

claim: Coupled with the proton gradient, stator–rotor interactions trigger large conformational changes required for flagellar rotation.
source: Coupled with the proton gradient, stator–rotor interactions trigger large conformational changes required for flagellar rotation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.
